vocabulary.body: The revealed Arabic text. When this page links to a verse, the Arabic is the Quran, and everything else is help understanding it.
An English rendering that carries the sense across. It helps you understand, and it is not itself the Quran.
Arabic sounds written out in English letters. Handy for practice, though your ear will learn more from a teacher or a reliable reciter.
Scholarly explanation of what a verse means, when it came, and what it asks of you. Reach for it when a verse feels difficult.

translationTips: Pick a translation where you can find out who translated it, who published it, and how they worked.
Readable English with footnotes beats an anonymous PDF or a screenshot someone posted.
Compare two translations when you are studying. If comparing them starts making you anxious, go back to one.
When a verse touches belief, worship, your family, your safety, or a decision you are about to make, ask a qualified teacher.

readingPaths.title: First sitting
readingPaths.body: Start with short chapters that double as prayer practice. Read the meaning slowly, then listen once. Leave your pronunciation alone for now.

readingPaths.title: Mercy and hope
readingPaths.body: Read this when shame or fear is louder than hope. Sit with what these verses say about how near Allah is and how ready to forgive, before you add anything else.

readingPaths.title: Prophets and purpose
readingPaths.body: Read Surah Yusuf a few pages at a time. It runs as one continuous story: a family that turns on him, long patience, temptation, prison, and forgiveness at the end.

readingPaths.title: Prayer and worship
readingPaths.body: Tie your reading to your prayer. These passages put prayer in its place: remembrance, a request for guidance, and somewhere to go when you need patience.

readingPaths.title: Character and patience
readingPaths.body: Keep this one practical. After you read, ask what it would change about how you speak, how patient you are, and how you treat people today.

weekPlan.title: Open with Al-Fatiha
weekPlan.body: Read the meaning of Al-Fatiha, then listen to it once. Carry the line about guidance with you through the day.

weekPlan.title: Learn the three short protectors
weekPlan.body: Read Al-Ikhlas, Al-Falaq, and An-Nas. Notice what they say about Allah being one, and about asking for protection. Do not try to memorize them today.

weekPlan.title: Read for hope
weekPlan.body: Read Quran 39:53 slowly. Then write one sentence, in your own words, about what Allah's mercy means for your situation.

weekPlan.title: Make your own dua
weekPlan.body: Read Quran 2:186 and 23:109. Then make a short dua in English, in your own words.

weekPlan.title: Connect Quran to prayer
weekPlan.body: Read Quran 20:14 and listen to Al-Fatiha again. Prayer is remembrance first. Getting it perfect comes later.

weekPlan.title: Practice patience
weekPlan.body: Read Quran 2:153 and Al-'Asr. Pick one small thing today where you will be patient, or tell the truth when it would be easier not to.

weekPlan.title: Review and ask one question
weekPlan.body: Go back to whichever passage stayed with you. If something confused you, write down the exact verse and take it to a teacher you trust.

resourceLinks.title: Quran.com
resourceLinks.body: Read, listen, compare translations, and open reciter pages from a browser, so there is nothing to install.

resourceLinks.title: The Clear Quran
resourceLinks.body: A readable English translation of the meaning. Use it to understand, and keep the Arabic as the Quran itself.

resourceLinks.title: New Muslim Academy
resourceLinks.body: Beginner classes and Quran help, written for people who are new to Islam.

resourceLinks.title: Mishari Rashid al-Afasy on Quran.com
resourceLinks.body: A clear reciter to listen along with. Listen through first, then repeat one short piece.

image.caption: Al-Fatihah, one line at a time.

stages: Week 1: one line of Al-Fatihah a day. Listen, repeat, and read the word meanings below. That is the only task.
Month 1: finish Al-Fatihah and add one short surah such as Al-Ikhlas. Keep praying with what you know, and learn what each phrase of the prayer means from the salah companion.

Month 3: start the Arabic letters and short vowels in a few short sessions a week, and add two or three more short surahs such as Al-Asr, Al-Kawthar, Al-Falaq and An-Nas. This is a good time to find a teacher, because a teacher hears sounds you cannot hear in yourself.
Month 6: read short surahs slowly from the page with a teacher checking you, and learn the meaning of everything you say in prayer.
Month 12: read steadily with the basic rules of tajweed, and if you want, start learning common Quranic words. Some people take longer, and that is fine.

plan.title: Making the plan work
notes: Reading and understanding are two different goals. Reading and reciting (the letters, then tajweed) is what you need for prayer. Understanding Arabic (vocabulary, then grammar) is a longer project you can take slowly.
Ten to fifteen minutes a day works better than one long session a week. The Prophet said the deeds Allah loves most are the regular ones, even if they are small.
Start with free options: a beginners' class at your masjid, the free New Muslim Academy Quran classes, or the free Madinah Arabic lessons linked below.

Paid tutoring is fine if you choose it freely. Book one trial class before paying for any package, and walk away from pressure, long prepaid bundles, a teacher with no name, or requests to move to private chat.
Pick one app or course at a time. Starting three apps and two courses at once usually ends with none.
You are not a lesser Muslim until you can read Arabic, and you do not pause your prayers until your recitation is perfect. The Prophet said the one who recites with difficulty gets a double reward.

sounds.title: Sounds to listen for
sounds.intro: English spelling uses the same letters for sounds that are different in Arabic. These are the ones English speakers most often find hard. Listen to a clear reciter for each one rather than relying on the spelling. A tajweed teacher can check the examples with you.

sounds.name: Ayn
sounds.tip: A squeeze deep in the throat. Transliteration often marks it with an apostrophe, as in na'budu (we worship).

sounds.name: Heavy h (ha)
sounds.tip: A breathy h from the middle of the throat, like breathing on cold glass. The h in al-hamdu is this letter, not the light h of "hat".

sounds.name: Kha
sounds.tip: The sound at the end of the Scottish "loch".

sounds.name: Ghayn
sounds.tip: Close to a French r, as in ghayril-maghdubi.

sounds.name: Qaf
sounds.tip: A k said further back in the throat, as in al-mustaqim.

sounds.name: The heavy letters
sounds.tip: Said with the back of the tongue raised, which darkens the vowel next to them. Listen for them in as-sirat and wa lad-dallin.

sounds.name: Two kinds of th
sounds.tip: One is the th in "thin", the other is the th in "this", as in alladhina.

sounds.name: Doubled letters (shaddah)
sounds.tip: Hold the letter a little longer, as in iyyaka and rabbil.

sounds.mistakesTitle: What if I get a letter wrong?
mistakes: Every learner makes mistakes, and the Prophet said the one who recites with difficulty gets a double reward. In the Shafi'i school, a letter mistake spoils that word, so you say the word again once, correctly. The prayer itself is only invalid when a mistake changes the meaning and was made on purpose.

A Hanafi answer, citing Ibn Abidin, says that mixing up letters such as saad and seen by accident does not invalidate the prayer, and that a learner should keep making a reasonable effort. Ask a teacher for the Maliki and Hanbali details.
Repeating a word again and again, or restarting the whole prayer over one uncertain letter, is not required. That kind of doubt (waswasa) is something to let go of.
practice: Pick one hard sound a week and practise it in a word you already say in prayer.
Once a week, record yourself reciting Al-Fatihah on your phone and compare it with the Quran.com audio.
Ask a teacher at your masjid to listen for five minutes and check just these letters. Most will be glad to.
Learn by listening. Transliteration is a reminder, not a replacement for hearing the word.
